title: Chapter 64: The Ashborn, Part 2 of 5: Kestrel
html:
She was tall.
That was the first thing. Taller than Corin, almost as tall as Oren, and thin in a hard way, like a rope that has been pulled tight for a long time. She had to stoop to come out under the flap of the tent, and when she straightened up on the other side of the fire, she stood very straight, with her shoulders back and her chin up, and the firelight went up her from the ground like water rising.
She wore the same gray-brown hide as everyone else, but hers was longer, a coat that came down to her knees, belted at the waist with a plaited strip of leather. Over her shoulders there was a cape of some pale fur, white or almost white, thick and soft. Her feet were wrapped in felt like the children's. Her hands were bare. She held them at her sides, loose, the fingers a little open.
Her head was shaved. Not cut short, like the others. Shaved, clean, right down to the skin, so that the firelight shone on the top of her skull. It made her look older than she was, or younger, Corin could not decide which. Past the middle of her life, perhaps. Perhaps not.
And the gray line on her face did not stop at the tip of her nose.
It began there, the same as everyone's. A finger's width of ash-gray down the middle of the face. But it did not begin at the forehead. It began further back. It came from the back of her head. From the nape of her neck, where it met the collar of her coat, up over the round bare skull in a straight gray stripe, over the crown, down the forehead, down the nose to the tip. As if someone had taken a brush and drawn one line, once, from the back of her neck to the end of her nose, all the way round, dividing her head into two halves.
It was not paint. Corin saw that as she came round the fire toward them. The children's lines had been paint. You could see the brush marks in them, the places where the ash was thicker or thinner. This was not. This was smooth and even and a little shiny, like the skin of an old scar, and it was not on her skin. It was her skin.
It was the same gray as his arm.
She stopped on the far side of the mats, a few steps away from them, and looked at them.
Her eyes were the color of tea. Strong tea, the kind Toby used to brew on the stove in the Harvesting Section at the end of a long night, brown and clear with a light in it. They went over Oren first, quickly, up and down, the way Arran's had. Then over Lyra. They stayed on Lyra a little longer, on her face and her black coat and her red scarf and her gloved hands, and something moved in them that Corin could not read.
Then they came to Corin.
And stayed.
She looked at him for a long time. At his face first. Then at his left arm, the sleeve of his coat, where the gray was hidden. She could not have seen it. His sleeve was down and buttoned at the wrist. But she looked at it anyway, at the exact place on his arm, a hand's width below the shoulder, where the gray stopped, as if she could see through the cloth. As if she could feel it, the way you can feel the heat of a stove across a room without touching it.
Then at his hands.
Then at his face again.
She did not touch the line on her own face, the way the others had done. She only looked at him.
"Ah," she said.
Her voice was low and dry, a little rough, as if it had been used a great deal outdoors, in the wind and the cold.
"We have one," she said, "who carries alone."
Nobody spoke.
She took one more step, onto the edge of the grass mats, and stood looking down at him from her height, and the firelight moved on the gray line on her skull.
"How many?" she said.
Corin did not understand. "How many what?"
"Inside you." She lifted one hand and turned it a little, in the air, toward his chest. Not touching. "How many do you carry? Not your own. Theirs."
He thought of the shelves. The rows and rows of them, in the back of his mind, in the place where he kept what he had taken. Years and years of taking. Mages and thieves and murderers and old women in back rooms. Pieces of them. Faces and voices and smells and hands. And the man in the coat who had been inside him for months. And Vivienne. Fresh and raw, five days old.
He could not feel the number. It was too big. All he could feel was the size of it. A great dark room full of shelves going back and back into the dark.
"I don't know," he said. "A lot."
Kestrel looked at him.
"Alone," she said. It was not a question.
"Yes."
She nodded, slowly, once. As if he had told her something she already knew and had hoped was not true.
"It is how they drown," she said.
She said it simply, quietly. The way you might say, it is how bread goes stale, or it is how the river floods in spring. A thing everyone knows. A thing that happens.
Beside him, Corin felt Lyra go very still.
"How who drown?" said Lyra.
Kestrel looked at her. The tea-colored eyes went over her face again, slowly.
"Ones like him," said Kestrel. "Who carry alone. They take one in. And then another. And another. And they keep them all in one room, by themselves. And the room fills up. And one day there is no air left in it. And they drown." She turned her eyes back to Corin. "We have seen it. Our grandmothers saw it. The old ones who carried alone, in the war. They came to the Glass, at the end. Walking. They did not know who they were anymore. They had too many in them. They walked out onto the Glass and they did not stop."
The hum came up through the ground. The fire hissed.
"We are not like that," said Kestrel. "We carry together. So nobody drowns."
She lifted her hand again, and this time she touched the gray line on her own skull. Not quickly, like the others. Slowly. Her fingers went to the back of her neck, and up over the crown of her head, and down her forehead and her nose to the tip, the whole length of it, all the way round. And when she took her hand away there was nothing on her fingers. No ash. Nothing came off.
"Sit," she said. "Eat. You have walked a long way, and you are on the edge of the Glass, and it is getting dark." She looked past them, up at the faint milky light in the sky beyond the ridge. "We do not talk about the dead in the dark until there is bread in your hands. That is the rule here."
She turned and went round the fire toward the gray tent.
Then she stopped, at the door of it, and looked back over her shoulder.
"They call this one Kestrel," she said, and touched her own chest. "We are the Ashborn. You are welcome at Last Thorn." A pause. Her eyes went to Corin's arm again, to the place under the sleeve. "All of you," she said. "Even the ones you have not named."
And she ducked in under the flap, and was gone.
The three of them stood there.
"Well," said Oren at last. His voice was very low. "That's a welcome."
The goat bleated at his knee.
Lyra had not moved. She was looking at the door of the gray tent where Kestrel had gone in. Her face in the firelight was very pale and very still, and her gloved hands were folded tight together in front of her, the fingers knotted.
"She knew," Lyra said. "About you. Before you said anything."
"Yes," said Corin.
"How?"
He did not answer.
He was thinking of the gray line. The smooth shiny scar-gray of it, from the back of her neck to the tip of her nose, that did not come off on her fingers. The same gray as his arm.
He did not know how she had known.
But he thought, perhaps, that she had known the way you know your own face in a mirror.
Bread, and the Glass at Your Back
They sat on the grass mats by the fire, and the Ashborn fed them.
It was the children who brought the food. The same three who had stopped them on the path, and others with them, more than he could count, small and round-headed and solemn, with the gray lines on their faces. They came out of the dark between the tents in a line, one behind the other, each of them carrying something in both hands, and they did not speak. They came to the edge of the mats, one by one, and knelt, and put down what they carried, and got up, and went back into the dark. It was done very carefully, the way children do a thing they have been taught and are proud of knowing.
There was bread first. The flat dark round loaves from the racks, three of them, still a little warm. Then a wooden bowl of something white and soft that turned out to be goat cheese, crumbly and sour and salty. Then a clay pot of broth, thick and brown, with lumps of meat in it and some kind of pale root, and a smell of herbs Corin did not know. Then three cups of horn, each one with a little hot dark tea in it that smelled of smoke. Then a bowl of something that looked like small black stones and turned out to be dried berries, sweet and hard and sticky.
The last child to come was the girl who had spoken on the path. The biggest one. She knelt in front of Corin with a little wooden dish held out flat on her two hands, and on the dish there was a single piece of bread. Not a loaf. A piece, torn off, about the size of a child's palm. It had been dipped in something. Honey, Corin thought. It shone in the firelight.
She held it out to him and did not move.
He looked at her. She looked back, very seriously, with her gray-striped face.
"Take it," said a voice from across the fire.
It was Arran. He had come out of the gray tent and was sitting on the far side of the fire, cross-legged on a mat, with his bone flute in his lap. He was not laughing now. His face in the firelight was quiet.
"It's the first bite," he said. "The guest has it. It's to say you're under our roof. Even though we've got no roof." He waved one long hand at the sky. "It's an old thing."
Corin took the bread off the dish. It was warm and sticky.
The girl stood up at once, and turned, and went away into the dark between the tents, and did not look back.
He ate it. It was sweet and sour together, and under the honey there was a taste of smoke, and something else. Something bitter and green, like a crushed leaf. He did not know what it was. He ate all of it and licked the honey off his fingers, and Arran watched him across the fire, and nodded once.
"Good," said Arran. "Now you can have the rest."
They ate.
Corin had not known how hungry he was. None of them had. They had eaten Granny Abbe's oatcake and the last of the cheese on the slope at midday, sitting on the gravel among the thorns, and nothing since, and before that they had walked from Haverstock across the high moor and up to the Lip and down again, and the cold had taken it all out of them. They ate the bread and the cheese and the broth, all three of them, without speaking, passing the pot and the bread between them. Oren tore the loaves in his big hands and gave the halves to the other two before he took any for himself. Lyra ate small quick bites, the way she always did, like a bird, and every now and then she stopped and looked round at the tents and the dark and the faint light in the sky over the ridge, and then went on eating.
The tea was smoky and bitter, and it was hot, and it went down into Corin's belly like a coal.
The goat had come too. It lay down on the gravel at the edge of the mats, close behind Oren, with its legs folded under it, and chewed and watched them with its yellow eyes. Every so often it put out its nose toward Oren's elbow, and Oren pushed it away without looking, and it put its nose back.
"He likes you," said Arran.
"He's a goat," said Oren.
"Yes. That's why it's worth something." Arran's bark of a laugh. "Goats don't like anybody."
People had begun to come close now. Not many. A few at a time, out of the dark, to stand at the edge of the light or to sit down on the far mats, near Arran, and look across the fire at the three strangers. Old men with their gray-patched faces. Women with babies. A young man and a young woman holding hands. They did not speak to the strangers. They spoke to each other, a little, quietly, in a way of talking that was the same tongue as the valleys, Corin thought, but rounder and slower, with the ends of the words cut off short.
And Corin noticed something.
They all sat the same way.
Every one of them who sat down, sat facing the same way. Not toward the fire. Not toward the strangers. Toward the ridge. Toward the north. Toward the faint milky light in the sky where the Glass was. Arran too. He sat on the south side of the fire, with his back to the camp and the thorn slope, and his face toward the ridge. They all did. The whole half-circle of them, on the far mats, sitting with their faces to the Glass, as if it were a fire too, a second one, bigger and colder, and they were warming themselves at it.
Corin looked round at his own side of the fire. He and Lyra and Oren had sat down on the north side, the side by the gray tent. With their backs to the ridge.
With their backs to the Glass.
He felt it then. He had not noticed it before. A kind of warmth on the back of his neck. Not like the warmth of the fire on his face. A different kind. Dry and steady and faintly prickling, the way the skin on your back feels when someone is standing behind you, close, not touching, just looking.
He turned his head and looked over his shoulder.
There was nothing there. Only the gray tent, and beyond it the low dark line of the gravel ridge, and above the ridge the milky shine in the sky. Nothing moved. But the feeling on the back of his neck did not go away.
Arran was watching him.
"You feel it," said Arran. It was not a question.
"Yes."
"Good. Some don't. The ones who don't, they're the ones that worry me." He lifted his chin toward the ridge. "We don't sit with our backs to it. Never. Not at a fire, not in a tent, not when we sleep. We always know where it is. It's the first thing the children learn, before they learn to walk. Before they learn their names. Where the Glass is." He looked at Corin, and then at Lyra, and then at Oren. "Kestrel's never once sat with her back to it. Not in her whole life. Not once."
"Why?" said Lyra.
Arran thought about it.
"Because it's always looking," he said simply. "And if you don't look back, it thinks you've forgotten it's there. And then it comes closer."
There was a silence round the fire.
"Is that true?" said Lyra.
Arran grinned at her. The white teeth in the firelight.
"I don't know," he said. "Nobody's ever been fool enough to find out."
Oren got up.
He did it without a word, and picked up his mat, and carried it round the fire, and put it down again on the south side, a little way along from Arran, and sat down on it, facing north. Toward the ridge. The goat got up and followed him and lay down again behind him.
Lyra looked at him. Then at Corin.
Then she got up too, and took her mat, and went round, and sat down beside Oren.
Corin sat for a moment longer, alone on the north side, with the warmth on the back of his neck.
Then he got up and went round the fire after them.
When he sat down, and looked up at the ridge, and the milky light above it, the feeling on his neck went away. And in its place there was another feeling. Smaller. Harder to name. Like the feeling of standing at the edge of a deep river at night, and knowing it is there, and not being able to see it.
Across the fire, at the door of the gray tent, Kestrel had come out again. She was standing in the doorway, tall and straight, in her long hide coat and her pale fur cape, looking at them. She had seen them move. Corin knew she had.
She did not smile. But she inclined her head to them, once, a very small movement of her shaved and lined skull.
Then she came round the fire, and sat down on the bare earth at the edge of the mats, between Arran and Corin, facing the Glass, and held out one hand for a piece of bread.
Lyra gave it to her.
And Kestrel ate, and drank a cup of the smoky tea, and did not speak until she had finished. When she had finished, she brushed the crumbs off her hands into the fire, carefully, the way you might brush crumbs off a table into your palm.
"Now," she said. "There is bread in your hands. Now we can talk about the dead."
The Ones We Carry
"When one of us is dying," said Kestrel, "we do not leave them alone."
She was sitting with her knees drawn up and her long arms folded round them, looking at the ridge. Her voice was low and even. The people on the far mats had gone quiet to listen, though they must have heard it a hundred times. Even the children had come back, and were sitting in a cluster at the edge of the light, very still, with their spears laid down on the gravel beside them.
"We come to the tent," said Kestrel. "All who can. Five. Ten. Twenty, if they are old and much loved. We sit round them. Close. Close enough to touch. And when they are ready, at the end, when they are going, they breathe out." She let a breath go herself, slowly, into the cold air, and it smoked white in the firelight and drifted away south. "The last breath. And the ones round them breathe in."
Nobody moved.
"And what is in the last breath," said Kestrel, "goes into us. Not all of it into one. A little into each. Some of the dying one's mornings into this one. Some of their winters into that one. Their mother's face into Kestrel. Their first goat into Arran." She glanced across at him, and Arran ducked his head and smiled a small smile at the fire. "We do not take. They give. It is their gift. The last one they make. And we carry it."
"And it doesn't..." Lyra stopped. She started again. "It doesn't hurt you? Having somebody else's things inside you?"
"It is heavy," said Kestrel. "Sometimes. In the first days. You wake in the night and you do not know your own tent, because for a moment it is their tent you are looking for. You reach for a hand that is not yours to reach for. You cry for a child you never had." She was quiet for a little. "But it is not much. Because it is only a little piece. And because the others are carrying the rest. And we talk about them. All of us. We sit at the fire and say, do you have her laugh? This one has her laugh. Do you have the day the river froze? This one has that. And so we pass them round, and nobody holds too much."
She put up her hand and touched the gray line on her face. Just the end of it, at the tip of her nose.
"This is where they go," she said. "Every one you carry, the gray goes a little further. The children paint it on, to show they will carry, when it is their time. The rest of us..." She lifted her chin toward the crowd on the far mats. The old man with the gray cheeks. The woman with the gray running down her throat. "The rest of us do not need to paint."
"And the handprints," said Corin. "On the tents."
"One for each." Kestrel did not look at the gray tent behind them. She did not have to. "When one of us dies, everyone who breathed them puts a hand in the ash of the fire, and presses it on their own tent. So we remember who is in there. So we can count them."
Corin thought of the tent behind them. The tent of hands. So covered in gray that no brown showed.
"That's your tent," he said.
"Yes."
He did not ask how many. He could not have felt the number, even if she had told him.
"It is how they drown," Kestrel said again, quietly, turning her head to look at him at last. "The ones who carry alone. They take a whole person, and put it in themselves, and nobody shares it with them. And then another. And they keep them all in one room, in the dark, and never speak of them. And the people inside them have nobody to talk to but each other. So they talk to each other. All night. And after a while the one who owns the room cannot hear himself over the noise of them."
The fire hissed. Somewhere among the tents, a goat bell clunked.
Corin did not say anything. He could not.
Because it was true. He knew it was true. The shelves at the back of his mind. The rows and rows of them, the faces and voices he had put there, one by one, and never once taken out and looked at, except when the Ministry asked him to. Kept in the dark. Kept quiet. And how, these last months, since the war started coming back to him in pieces, the shelves had not been quiet. How some nights he lay in his room at the top of the tenement on Tallow Street and could not sleep for the sound of them. Not voices, exactly. More like the hum of the Glass. A low steady noise under everything, like a crowd in another room.
Kestrel was watching his face.
Then she did a strange thing.
She leaned toward him. Not much. Just a little, from where she sat, so that her face came closer to his, and she breathed in through her nose. Slowly. The way a cook breathes over a pot to know if it is done.
And her face changed.
It went still. Very still. Then her lips came together, tight, and her nostrils went thin, and she sat back again, slowly, away from him.
"Who is that?" she said.
Corin's heart was going hard. "Who?"
"The fresh one." Kestrel did not take her eyes off him. "The new one. On top. You have not been carrying her long." She breathed in again, from where she was, more carefully. "Days. A few days."
He knew who she meant.
Vivienne.
Lady Vivienne, in the big bed with the violet curtains, in the old stone room by the fish market wall, on the night of the masks. Tiny and bald and toothless, with her wig on its stand and her necklace of little glowing vials laid out on a cloth, and the gray up to her elbows. Remy asleep on the narrow bed by the door. And Corin sitting beside her, because he had promised the boy he would, with his hands on her face, at the end, taking it. All of it. As fast as it came. So that it would not go into Remy. Five days ago. Six. He had lost count.
He had not sorted what he had taken. He had not dared. It had gone into the empty room at the front of his mind, the one where Lyra used to be, and filled it up from wall to wall, and he had shut the door on it and walked away north.
"A woman," he said. His voice was not quite steady. "She's dead."
"Yes," said Kestrel. "We can smell that."
She was quiet for a moment, with her head a little on one side, as if she were listening to something far off.
"A woman who sold children," she said.
Lyra drew in her breath, sharp.
Kestrel did not look at her. She was still looking at Corin, and her eyes were narrow, and there was something in them that was not anger and not pity. Something harder. The look of a person who has smelled a bad thing many times before, and has never got used to it.
"A great many children," said Kestrel. "For a long time. Her hands smell of coin. And of the lamps. And of a little box with a lock on it." She breathed in again. Slower. Deeper. Her eyes half closed. "And under that..."
She stopped.
Corin waited.
"Under that," said Kestrel softly, "a girl who gutted fish."
The fire cracked.
"A little girl," said Kestrel. "On a wet stone, by the water, with a knife too big for her. And the cold. And her hands red. And somebody shouting at her to be quicker." She opened her eyes. "She is very far down. Under all the rest. Under all the children. But she is there. You took her too. You took all of it, in a hurry. The fish girl and the woman who sold children. Both. All mixed together, and nobody to help you sort them."
She sat back and folded her arms round her knees again, and looked at the ridge.
"That is a heavy one to carry alone," she said. "For a man who already carries so much."
Nobody said anything for a long time.
Corin sat and looked at the fire. His hands were shaking. He put them flat on his knees to stop them, and they went on shaking, a little, under his palms.
He had known about the fish girl. Somewhere. The wet stone and the knife and the red hands were in him, with all the rest.
But he had never once let himself think of her as a child.
Beside him Lyra had gone white. Not pale. White, like paper. She was staring at the fire too, and her lips were pressed together, hard, and he knew what she was thinking of. He knew because he was thinking of it too. Of the children in the cellars. Of the rows of little beds. Of her own father's hand in his, and the stairs, and the counting.
And of Vivienne.
Vivienne, who had been a little girl once. On a wet stone. With a knife too big for her.
"I didn't know," said Lyra at last. Her voice was very small. "I didn't know she was ever..." She stopped. "I didn't want to know."
"No," said Kestrel. "Nobody does." She looked at Lyra for a long moment, sideways, across Corin. "But they always were. Every one. That is the hardest thing we learn, carrying. That every one of them was a child once, on a wet stone somewhere. Even the worst." She turned back to the ridge. "Especially the worst."
